'''''Eucalyptus obliqua''''', commonly known as '''messmate stringybark'''<ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian H. |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus obliqua'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/080ef661-c542-4ae3-94d0-9e57c3629818 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Victoria |access-date=18 November 2019}}</ref> or '''messmate''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus obliqua'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~obliqua |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=18 November 2019}}</ref> but also known as '''brown top''', '''brown top stringbark''', '''stringybark''' or '''Tasmanian oak''',<ref name="APCND">{{cite web | title = Australian Plant Common Name Database | url  = http://www.anbg.gov.au/common.names/ | publisher = [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]] | access-date = 2007-07-15}}</ref> is a species of tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern Australia. It has rough, stringy or fibrous bark on the trunk and larger branches, smooth greyish bark on the thinnest branches, lance-shaped to curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven to fifteen or more, white flowers and cup-shaped or barrel-shaped fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus obliqua'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|90|m}} or sometimes a [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] and forms a [[lignotuber]]. The trunk is up to {{cvt|3|m}} in diameter and has thick, rough, stringy or fibrous bark. Branches more than {{cvt|80|mm}} in diameter have stringy bark and thinner branches have smooth greenish or greyish bark. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have glossy green, broadly egg-shaped to lance-shaped leaves that are {{cvt|60-210|mm}} long and {{cvt|23-85|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are the same shade of glossy green on both sides, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|60-220|mm}} long and {{cvt|15-70|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|7-34|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of between seven and fifteen or more on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|4-25|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|3-8|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to club-shaped, {{cvt|4-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with a conical to rounded [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs in most months and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, cup-shaped to barrel-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|6-12|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-11|mm}} wide with the valves near rim level.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus obliqua'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_obliqua.htm |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=31 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus obliqua'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20obliqua |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=18 November 2019}}</ref> The tallest known specimen in Tasmania is {{cvt|86|m}} tall.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.gianttrees.com.au | title = Giant Trees | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070216110313/http://www.gianttrees.com.au/ | archive-date = 2007-02-16 }}</ref> Trees up to {{cvt|98.8|m}} tall have been recorded.<ref>Carder, A. 2005: Giant Trees of Western America and The World. Harbour Publishing, Madeira Park, Canada.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus obliqua'' was collected in 1777 by [[David Nelson (botanical collector)|David Nelson]] and [[William Anderson (naturalist)|William Anderson]] during [[James Cook|Cook]]'s third expedition, and was the first eucalyptus species to be formally described.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Costermans |first1=L. F. |title=Trees of Victoria: a fully illustrated guide to the recognition of some 85 trees and large shrubs native to Victoria and three neighbouring states |date=1973 |publisher=L.F. Costermans |location=East Kew, Vic. |isbn=0-9599105-0-6 |page=47 |edition=3rd}}</ref> The collections were made at Adventure Bay on [[Bruny Island]] in what is now Tasmania. The specimens were sent to the [[British Museum]] in [[London]], where they were examined by [[Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle]]. L'Héritier recognised the specimens as belonging to a new genus which he called ''Eucalyptus'' and gave the name ''Eucalyptus obliqua'' to the species. The [[Type (biology)|type species]] is therefore ''E. obliqua''. L'Héritier published the first formal description in 1789 in his book ''Sertum Anglicum''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus obliqua''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455969|publisher=APNI|access-date=18 November 2019}}</ref><ref>{{ cite book | last=L'Héritier | first=Charles Louis  | author-link=Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle | year=1788 | title=Sertum Anglicum, seu, Plantae rariores quae in hortis juxta Londinum: imprimis in horto regio Kewensi excoluntur, ab anno 1786 ad annum 1787 observatae  | place=Paris | publisher=Petri Francisci Didot | page=11 | language=la | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11832429 }}</ref><ref name="ANBG1">{{cite web |title=Anderson, William (1750 - 1788) |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/biography/anderson-william.html |publisher=Council of Heads of Australasian Herbaria Australian National Herbarium |access-date=18 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="ANBG2">{{cite web |title=Nelson, David (? - 1789) |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/biography/nelson-david.html |publisher=ouncil of Heads of Australasian Herbaria Australian National Herbarium |access-date=18 November 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''obliqua'') is from the [[Latin]] ''obliquus'' ("oblique"), in reference to the leaf bases of unequal length.<ref name="History of Eucalyptus">{{cite web | title = The History of Eucalyptus | url = http://www.anbg.gov.au/cpbr/cd-keys/Euclid/sample/html/history.htm | work = EUCLID: Eucalypts of southern Australia (Second Edition) | access-date = 2007-07-15 | archive-date = 2016-03-04 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304090756/http://www.anbg.gov.au/cpbr/cd-keys/Euclid/sample/html/history.htm }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Messmate stringybark is widespread in cooler areas of south eastern Australia. It occurs from [[Kangaroo Island]], through southeast [[South Australia]], throughout [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[Tasmania]], mainly east of the tablelands in [[New South Wales]], with a few populations extending into southern [[Queensland]]. Thus the overall range of latitude is 28–43{{frac|1|2}}°S. It occurs from sea level up to elevations of {{cvt|1475|m}} in the [[Northern Tablelands]] of New South Wales. The climate is humid or subhumid, with temperatures ranging from cool to warm, and annual rainfall ranging from {{cvt|500 to 2400|mm}}. Severe winter frosts are common, severe drought extremely uncommon.<ref name="Boland 1984">{{cite book | author = Boland, D. J. | year = 1985 | title = Forest Trees of Australia | edition = 4th | isbn = 0-643-05423-5|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

It occurs on a wide range of soils in hilly or mountainous areas. In cool mountainous areas it forms open-forest with other ''Eucalyptus'' species such as ''[[Eucalyptus fastigata|E. fastigata]]'' (brown barrel), ''[[Eucalyptus nitens|E. nitens]]'' (shining gum), ''[[Eucalyptus cypellocarpa|E. cypellocarpa]]'' (mountain grey gum), ''[[Eucalyptus viminalis|E. viminalis]]'' (manna gum) and ''[[Eucalyptus delegatensis|E. delegatensis]]'' (alpine ash).<ref name="Boland 1984"/>

==Uses==
One of the most important Australian hardwoods, ''E. obliqua'' is often sold with ''[[Eucalyptus regnans|E. regnans]]'' (mountain ash) as [[Victorian ash]] or [[Tasmanian oak]] depending on its origin. It is slightly denser  than ''E. regnans''  – estimates of density range from {{cvt|720 to 830|kg/m}}. The sapwood is pale brown, the heartwood light brown. It has an even texture, with straight grains sometimes interlocked, and well-defined rings. Gum veins are common.<ref name="Boland 1984"/><ref name="Bootle 1983">{{cite book | author = Bootle, Keith R. | title = Wood in Australia: types, properties and uses | year = 1983 | location = Sydney | publisher = McGraw-Hill | isbn = 0-07-451047-9}}</ref>

The timber has moderate hardness and strength, but low durability. It splits easily, and is easily worked, glued and stained; it is also suitable for steam bending. It is mostly used for pulp production and for construction and manufacture, especially in house building, joinery, flooring, and furniture.<ref name="Boland 1984"/><ref name="Bootle 1983"/>
